A toponymic study · Senegal · 11,789 places

What Senegal's
villages are called

A village name records the language, the lineage, the faith and the landscape that were present the day it was founded — not the day you read it. Read all of them at once and the map starts admitting things.

F1

The villages that come in pairs

Across Senegal, dozens of localities exist twice or three times over — one name, repeated with a different ethnic label appended. Khaye Sérèr sits 330 metres from Khaye Ouolof. Ndiafat exists as Wolof, Sérèr and Peul.

These are not duplicates in the data. They are neighbouring settlements that chose to distinguish themselves by ethnicity rather than by name — communities sharing a locality, a water point and a name, while keeping the distinction legible in the map itself.

The distances are the striking part. If these were unrelated villages that happened to share a name, they would be scattered at random across the country. They are not: the median gap is under two kilometres. They are next door to each other.

How far apart are the twins?

Read with care. An ethnonym in a name records how a settlement was distinguished when it was named. It is not a census, and it says nothing about who lives there now.

F2

A frontier you can draw

Several Senegalese languages have a word meaning roughly "the home of", used to build village names. Wolof uses Keur. Pulaar uses Saré. Mandinka suffixes -kounda. They mean the same thing, so where each one is used is not a question of meaning — it is a question of who was naming.

Mapped, they do not overlap. They partition the country.

Settlement morphemes: same meaning, different language, different territory.
MorphemeLanguageSenseVillagesCentreHeartland

Read with care. This is a map of naming, not of speech. A Keur village is Wolof-named; that is not the same as Wolof-speaking, and the gap between the two is exactly where the history is. Confirming any of it belongs to historians and linguists.

F3

Pulaar does not agree with itself

The result that did not appear in any plan. Pulaar speakers do not use a single word for their settlements — they use several, and each one occupies its own territory.

Saré holds the south, in Kolda and Sédhiou — historically Fuladu. Ouro and Gourel hold the east, in Tambacounda and Matam — the Fouta Toro and the Ferlo. Loumbel and Belel sit further north again. The centres are hundreds of kilometres apart and barely overlap.

One language, one meaning, three separate vocabularies, three separate territories. The most economical reading is that these are distinct settlement histories that never merged — which is what historians say about Fouta Toro and Fuladu, arrived at here from nothing but names.

Where each Pulaar morpheme sits
Centre of gravity of every village using each word

Read with care. Belel and Loumbel carry medium-confidence glosses. The geographic separation is solid; the precise sense of each word is the part that needs a Pulaar speaker's judgement.

F4

The shadow of Touba

Hundreds of Senegalese villages carry a name of Arabic and Sufi origin — Darou (an abode), Touba (blessedness), Madina, Taïba, Missira, Maka. If these names were simply part of the national vocabulary, they would be spread evenly. They are not.

Measured as a share of all villages in each ring of distance from Touba, the density falls away from the city in a clean gradient — highest in the first 25 kilometres, roughly a third of that by 75 kilometres out.

The religious settlement of the peanut basin is well described by historians and geographers. What is added here is the measurement: the front is visible in the naming record, and it has a shape.

Sufi-named villages by distance from Touba
Share of all villages in each 25 km ring
Sufi and Islamic name elements found in the corpus.
ElementSenseVillagesConfidence

Read with care. Distance rings far from Touba contain few villages, so their rates are noisy. The gradient is trustworthy within roughly 150 km; beyond that the line is thin.

F5

Villages that split in two

A second population of adjacent same-name villages exists, produced by an entirely different mechanism: numbering. Keur X Un and Keur X Deux — a settlement that divided, or was divided, and took French ordinals to tell the halves apart.

The striking thing is the comparison with F1. Two unrelated processes — ethnic co-settlement and administrative fission — produce neighbouring villages at almost exactly the same spacing. Whatever sets the distance between two Senegalese villages that share ground appears not to care why they are separate.

The closest numbered village splits.
LocalityPartsRegionGap (km)

Read with care. French ordinals point to the colonial and post-colonial administration as the likely agent, but the data cannot date a split. Treat the mechanism as a hypothesis and the spacing as the measurement.

F6

Where the family names settled

Around a fifth of Senegalese village names end in a family name — Keur Massar, the home of Massar. Each is a founder, remembered in the map. Aggregated, they give something no register holds: the geographic footprint of a lineage.

For anyone in the diaspora tracing a name, this is the practical output of the whole study.

Family names appearing in village names, with the centre and heartland of each. Group attribution marks the most common association only — many names are shared across communities.
Family nameMost associated withVillagesHeartland

Read with care. Surnames cross ethnic lines constantly in Senegal. Rows marked shared are common to several communities and the group label should be treated as a tendency, never as an identity.

The grammar

How the names are built

Senegalese place names are compounds, and the parts combine by rule. Each node is a name element; each link means the two appear together in a real village name. What emerges is the combinatorial grammar of the naming system — the settlement words at the centre, the founder names radiating out. Drag to explore.

An open thread

The trees in the names

Some names record a landscape rather than a person: Gouye is the baobab, Dakhar the tamarind, Wendou a Pulaar pond. A village called for a baobab was named by people who could see one.

That makes these names a potential record of vegetation and water that may no longer be there — a proxy for ecological change, written before anyone was measuring it.

This study stops at the map. Testing it needs current land-cover and hydrology data to overlay, which was not reachable from the build environment. The layer is published as a hypothesis, not a result — the honest state of it.

Methods and limits

What this is, and what it is not

The corpus. 11,789 populated places from the GeoNames Senegal dump, licensed ODbL. Region and department were assigned by point-in-polygon against geoBoundaries ADM1/ADM2 polygons, which resolved of places — the source's own department field covered only 18%.

The tagging. Names are split into elements, spelling variants are collapsed (Sintiou / Sinntiou / Sintiân / Santiou are treated as one morpheme), and each element is matched against a hand-built lexicon. Every gloss carries a confidence level, shown in the tables. Roughly of names carry at least one recognised element; the rest are unclassified and are not silently assigned.

What it is not. GeoNames is not the Senegalese state. This has not been cross-checked against the ANSD census — that remains the most valuable next step, and until it happens, treat every count as approximate. Coverage is uneven and spellings are inconsistent, so morpheme counts are floors, not totals.

Above all: a pattern in names is a hypothesis about history, never a demonstration of it. Nothing here proves a migration, a language shift or a conversion. It shows where the map is worth asking a historian, a linguist or an elder about — and it points at several places nobody appears to have asked yet.
